cards.title: Maximum influence of polynomial threshold functions
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal:
Determine, up to universal multiplicative constant factors jointly in \(n\) and \(d\), the function
\[M(n,d)=\max\{I(f):f\in\mathcal F_{n,d}\},\qquad n,d\in\mathbb N,\quad n\ge1,\quad1\le d\le n,\]
where \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) is the class of Boolean functions represented by the sign of a real polynomial of total degree at most \(d\) with no zero on \(\{-1,1\}^n\), and \(I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution, defined below. The answer must give a positive growth function \(h(n,d)\) and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of both parameters, such that \[\forall n\ge1\ \forall d\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad c\,h(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le C\,h(n,d).\] No particular formula for \(h\) or extremizing Boolean function is prescribed.
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A real multilinear polynomial of degree at most \(d\) has the form
\[p(x)=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\|S|\le d}}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\qquad a_S\in\mathbb R,\]
with empty product \(1\). All coefficients are unrestricted reals; there is no bound on their magnitude, bit length, the number of nonzero monomials, or the minimum nonzero value of \(|p|\) on the cube. Require \(p(x)\ne0\) at every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\). Its threshold function is \(f(x)=+1\) when \(p(x)>0\), and \(f(x)=-1\) when \(p(x)<0\). The class \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) contains every function with at least one such representation, not just those whose least possible threshold degree is exactly \(d\). Starting with arbitrary real polynomials gives the same class: reducing powers using \(x_i^2=1\) preserves the cube values and does not increase degree. Excluding zeros fixes the tie convention; any representation using one fixed value of sign at zero can be perturbed by a sufficiently small constant to remove its cube zeros without changing the function.

Choose \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) cube points, with independent equally likely coordinates. For \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) have coordinate \(-x_i\) at \(i\) and agree with \(x\) elsewhere. Define
\[\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}|\{x:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\quad s_f(x)=|\{i\in[n]:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\]
\[I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}s_f(x).\]
Thus total influence is average sensitivity, not maximum pointwise sensitivity and not influence divided by \(n\). There is no biased input distribution or additional probability over polynomials. The maximization is over Boolean functions; different coefficient choices representing the same function have the same influence. It is a maximum rather than merely a supremum because only finitely many Boolean functions exist on a fixed cube, and \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) is nonempty. Constants belong to the class with influence zero, while a dictator \(f(x)=x_1\) has influence one; hence \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain.

The constants in the answer must be absolute: they cannot depend on degree, dimension, a representation, or an asymptotic path through the parameter pairs. The estimates must hold throughout the domain, including small dimensions and growing degrees; finite exceptional cases must be covered by the proved constants. This is a mathematical extremal-growth problem, with no evaluation-time requirement or finite encoding assumption for real coefficients. The omitted degree-zero case has value zero, and degrees larger than \(n\) give no additional Boolean functions, so the displayed domain covers all nontrivial regimes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a specified growth function \(h\) and universal positive constants \(c,C\), together with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both inequalities for every stated \((n,d)\). The upper bound must cover every realizing polynomial in the defined class. The lower bound must establish, for each pair, the existence of a degree-at-most-\(d\) threshold function with influence at least \(c h(n,d)\); an algorithm for producing its coefficients is not required. The answer must determine joint growth, including the large-degree saturation regime. Merely renaming \(M\), repeating its defining maximization, or giving an equivalent optimization is not such a determination. A degree-dependent hidden factor, a polylogarithmic gap in \(n\), a result only for fixed \(d\), or a counterexample to one proposed formula without matching replacement bounds is insufficient. No exact symmetric maximizer is required. The accepted precision is universal constant factors, not additive error \(1/100\).
cards.why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.

importance.reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.

progress.text: Kane proves the \(\sqrt n\) exponent up to logarithmic factors depending on degree; the preprint, CCC presentation and journal version have different dates.
Kim–Maldonado–Wellens establish influence estimates for structured quadratic coefficient graphs.
Chapman disproves the original exact extremizer conjecture while preserving the asymptotic open question.
Chapman’s MIT thesis again distinguishes the exact, asymptotic and weaker polylogarithmic formulations.
Kothari and coauthors’ revised rational-degree paper restates the conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue in §5.2.
Chang and coauthors’ second revision proves polylogarithmic Boolean surface area for fixed-degree PTFs, a different moment from total influence.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture is false, but no universal joint constant-factor determination of M(n,d) was found in the bounded primary-source review. The surviving O(d sqrt(n)) influence bound is explicitly still a conjecture in the checked April2026 revisions. The Boolean surface-area theorem bounds a different sensitivity moment with degree-dependent logarithmic factors, and the rational-degree theorem concerns a different degree comparison. New proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: The target is the maximum total influence as a joint function of dimension and threshold degree, within universal constant factors. It retains the quantitative formulation selected in the earlier review. The asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture is a proposed answer at a particular scale; the stronger claim prescribing an exact symmetric maximizer is a separate, disproved statement.

A polynomial threshold function evaluates a real polynomial and keeps its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority and weighted voting rules; degree two also permits pairwise interactions. Threshold degree measures the degree needed to represent the sign pattern, rather than the degree needed to equal the Boolean function numerically on every input.

Total influence is the expected number of sensitive coordinates at a uniformly random input. If \(D(f)\) is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2^{1-n}D(f)\). By contrast, the probability that flipping one uniformly chosen coordinate changes the output is \(I(f)/n\). The normalization in the target is the former, which ranges from zero to \(n\).

For odd \(n\), majority has \[I(\operatorname{MAJ}_n)=n\,2^{1-n}\binom{n-1}{(n-1)/2}\sim\sqrt{2n/\pi}.\] Thus influence already grows with dimension at degree one. At the opposite endpoint, parity \(f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) has degree \(n\) and influence \(n\), so \(M(n,n)=n\).

The classical symmetric examples change sign across consecutive central Hamming layers. Their total influence has order \(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\}\), with constants uniform in the two parameters. This supplies the standard lower scale, including saturation at large degree. Gotsman and Linial conjectured that such an example actually maximizes influence exactly; the remaining asymptotic question permits different maximizers.

Chapman’s counterexamples refute that exact assertion for \(d=2\) in every odd dimension \(n\ge5\), and for \(n\ge7\) with \(3\le d\le n-3\). They do not rule out a universal \(O(d\sqrt n)\) upper bound. Combined with the elementary upper bound \(I(f)\le n\) and the standard lower scale, that surviving conjecture would give \(M(n,d)=\Theta(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\})\).

The common constants are part of the mathematical target. Bounds \(M(n,d)\le C_d\sqrt n\) with an unspecified degree-dependent constant \(C_d\) do not determine the joint dependence on \(n,d\). Nor does an estimate only as \(n\to\infty\) with \(d\) fixed cover sequences of increasing degree. The requested bound must also cover the transition to influence of order \(n\).

Kane’s Theorem 2 gives \(I(f)\le\sqrt n\,(\log n)^{O(d\log d)}2^{O(d^2\log d)}\) for \(d\ge2\). For every fixed degree this has the correct power of \(n\), up to logarithmic factors. Those factors still grow with dimension, and the bound’s dependence on degree is much larger than linear, so it does not give matching universal factors in the requested joint regime.

For quadratic threshold functions, Kim, Maldonado and Wellens study the graph whose edges mark nonzero coefficients of pairwise monomials. Their Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 give bounds in terms of the graph’s fractional chromatic number and its number of edges. These are structural estimates for a prescribed representation, not a matching bound for all dense quadratic representations.

The April 27, 2026 revision by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a fixed-degree polylogarithmic bound on Boolean surface area, defined by \(\operatorname{BSA}(f)=\mathbb E_x\sqrt{s_f(x)}\). Its Theorem 1.1 has constants depending on degree. The paper explicitly distinguishes this fractional sensitivity moment from total influence \(\mathbb E_x s_f(x)\).

The two quantities satisfy \((\operatorname{BSA}(f))^2\le I(f)\le\sqrt n\,\operatorname{BSA}(f)\). In particular, an upper bound on Boolean surface area cannot be squared to obtain an upper bound on influence. The checked 2026 surface-area theorem therefore still leaves dimension-dependent logarithmic factors when applied to this target.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision establishes a polynomial relationship between rational degree and ordinary degree. Its §5.2 restates the asymptotic influence conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue. Neither that main degree theorem nor the proposed weaker conjecture determines the maximum influence of arbitrary polynomial threshold functions.

A matching joint bound would quantify how strongly a low-degree sign representation constrains the edge boundary of a Boolean function. This connects algebraic representation to sensitivity, noise behavior and learning-theoretic complexity. A solution may establish the surviving conjectured scale or a different scale, but disproving one particular candidate without determining the extremal growth does not complete the task.

sentences: A polynomial threshold function records the sign of a real polynomial on the uniformly distributed Boolean cube.
Total influence is the expected number of individual coordinate flips that change the function’s value.
The target is the largest influence possible as a joint function of dimension and degree bound, within constants independent of both parameters.
A complete Lean proof must give a matching universal upper bound and a lower example for every parameter pair, including the regime where influence is of order the dimension.
The disproved exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture, fixed-degree logarithmic bounds and the separate 2026 surface-area and rational-degree theorems do not determine this joint growth.

Read the full MIT thesis title metadata (September2022) and Chapter6 Conjectures6.1.1–6.1.3 and Theorems6.1.1/6.1.2. It again separates exact, asymptotic and weak logarithmic formulations. Only the relevant chapter passages were reviewed, not the whole thesis.

Read Kane arXiv:1210.1283v1 introduction and Theorem2. It bounds influence by sqrt(n) times (log n) to O(d log d) and2 to O(d² log d), with the central-layer comparison for n much larger than d². Official arXiv dates the preprint4 October2012; the downloaded PDF’s compilation date is2 November2018. The author repository and primary-paper bibliographies confirm Computational Complexity23(2)2014,151–175, following CCC2013.

Read Kim–Maldonado–Wellens arXiv:1709.06650v1 abstract, introduction, Theorems1.1–1.3 and the majority influence discussion. The coefficient-graph bounds are for quadratic PTFs and depend on graph parameters. Standard cube-edge counting and binomial concentration give the stated saturation of the known symmetric lower scale; this is existing elementary context, not a new extremal theorem.

Read Chang–Slote–Volberg–Zhang arXiv:2604.08095v2 full abstract, §1, Theorem1.1 and Proposition2.3. The theorem gives BSA at most32(log(en))^(2K_d+1) for fixed degree, with K_d degree-dependent; its sensitivity tail estimate does not remove the influence gap. Official history confirms v1 9 April and v2 27 April2026 and the revised four-author list. The moment-comparison inequalities were checked directly; full new-paper proof not independently certified.

Read Kothari–Kovacs-Deak–Wang–Yang arXiv:2601.08727v2 abstract and §5.2 Conjecture2; compared the corresponding ECCC TR26-005 revision1 passage. The8 April2026 revision restates the threshold-degree influence conjecture while proving a different rational/ordinary-degree theorem. The older unnumbered report has different section numbers; §5.2 belongs to the checked revision.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
